style: Say in a friendly, youthful way, like a helpful older student
lines: Pick a scene. You'll choose what to say, and you can rewind any line to try it another way.
Build an I-statement. Pick one tile for each part, then check your line.
Grab a partner. One of you is the Speaker, one is the Listener. Then swap.
Say how you feel, what happened and what you need.
Say back their feeling and their reason before you answer.
Look for a plan that works for both of you.
See the faded line? That was last time. Compare how they react.
A feeling is one word, like hurt or worried. 'I feel like you' is a thought, not a feeling.
Listener, say back what you heard before you share your side.
You worked it out.
Okay for now.
Still stuck. Try rewinding a line.
Clean run. Every move was a strong one.
I-statement. You said how you feel, what happened and what you need, without blaming. That is easier to hear.
Half an I-statement. You named a feeling, but not what you need. Add an ask.
You-statement. It starts with what they did wrong, so people usually defend themselves.
Brush-off. It avoids the fight now, but the problem is still there.
Reflective listen. You said back their feeling and their reason. They can tell you heard them.
Fix it too fast. You jumped to a solution before showing you heard them.
Yeah-but. You went back to your side before they finished theirs.
Dismiss. Telling someone their reason doesn't count makes them dig in.
Both-sides plan. It meets your need and theirs.
Ask what works. Inviting their idea makes it a plan you made together.
Give in. It ends the argument, but your need disappears. Try one that works for both.
Demand. An order, not a plan. It usually starts the fight again.
